issues.root_cause:
AA-CIS-App api/core/aa544_tenant_pool.py:309. `_read_flag` wraps `redis.get(flag_key)` in `asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=FLAG_READ_TIMEOUT_S)`, and FLAG_READ_TIMEOUT_S is 0.5 s (line 160). The timeout branch logs `aa817_tenant_flag_read_failed reason=timeout` at ERROR (line 311), then returns True, which keeps the request on the tenant pool. That is the fail-closed outcome designed in S241 D-12. None of the flags involved (aa859:t2_version_reads_pool, aa859:integration_connect_pool, aa986:tenant_notifications_pool) is pinned OFF, so the result is the same as a successful read: the request gets the tenant pool and answers normally. The only extra cost is up to 0.5 s of latency.

Why the read times out: the outer bound is the same as the client's own bound. api/core/redis_client.py:27 sets socket_timeout to 0.5 s, and line 39 adds one retry on timeout (Retry(NoBackoff(), 1), retry_on_timeout=True). So when a socket operation is slow, the outer wait_for cancels the call at 0.5 s, at the same moment the client would start its retry. The retry was added for stale pooled connections and new connects, but here it can never finish.

When it happens: every event is the first tenant request on a freshly deployed task. The events come 13 to 80 minutes after the release commit, each on a different task and release, from the same E2E tenant. Several routes fire together (pool, notifications and my-versions in the same second). api/main.py:148 builds the Redis client lazily and never pings it at startup, so this cold burst opens new TLS + AUTH connections to ElastiCache (REDIS_TLS) while the event loop does its first-request work. In the same request, the rate-limit middleware GET and INCRBY finish in 2 to 9 ms. Only the flag GET goes past 0.5 s.

The ERROR level matters in two places. Sentry turns each line into an issue event. The AA-CIS-Infra CloudWatch alarm also e-mails on any `aa817_tenant_flag_read_failed` line, so most deploys raise a false alarm.

The T8 angle call ran out of output tokens, so its reply was cut off. The code then misread the cut reply as a reply with too few angles.

At the failing release 8137655 (05/11 13:39 UTC), services/acp_angle_gate/generate.py:135 sent the t8_angle_gen request with a fixed max_tokens=2048. Route v6 serves Sonnet 5.5, which writes longer replies, so the reply stopped at that 2048-token limit. In the event payload, angle 2's best_final_style breaks off mid-sentence at "...only as brief context for", and there is no angle 3.

_parse_response (generate.py:62-69) catches the json.loads failure and lets json_repair rebuild the cut JSON. The result is an `angles` list with only 2 entries. _validate (generate.py:73-76) then raises "Expected exactly 3 angles". At that release nothing checked stop_reason and nothing retried a cut reply. The job failed on attempt 2 of 2 (job_kind t8_angles, attempt=2, next_status=failed), and the T8 request ended with no angles.

The job did not crash. Its second and last attempt (attempt 2 of 2, max_attempts=2 at services/jobs/recompute_job.py:176) waited 1,800 s for the platform recompute advisory lock. When the wait ran out, services/export/handler.py:251 raised RecomputeLockTimeout. The worker counts that as a final failure (next_status=failed) and logs it with log.exception at error level (shared/jobs/worker.py, job_failed).

Mechanism. The cap of one running recompute is global: queue.claim counts the rows with status='running'. So while attempt 2 was running, no other recompute row could be running. The lock holder must have been an orphan: a recompute thread whose job attempt had already ended in the DB but which was still alive.

How an orphan forms. The run sits in asyncio.to_thread (recompute_job.py:~240). A CancelledError there only sets the stop event (recompute_job.py:247-249). Three paths cause that cancel: lease lost, the reaper, or an admin cancel. The thread checks the stop event only between stages (services/recompute/stages.py:401). Until then it keeps the session advisory lock on its own connection (handler.py:246).

The reaper puts the row back in the queue with run_after=now() and no release delay (queue.reap). So the next attempt is claimed at once and starts waiting behind its own earlier attempt. A platform recompute really takes about 16-52 minutes (lessons.md:107, S281). The wait budget is set to the same value as the expected run time (LOCK_MAX_WAIT_SECONDS = EXPECTED_SECONDS = 1800, recompute_job.py:71-72), which is shorter than one real run. As a result the waiter gives up on a holder that is alive and still working, and the code describes that holder as 'stuck' (errors.py docstring). Attempt 1 left no Sentry error, which points to the lease-lost or reap path.

issues.root_cause: This error did not come from app code. It came from a one-off operator script run through ECS exec on 03/11: /tmp/20261103T043042-489038-d2_live.py. The tools/ecs/ecsx.sh wrapper names runs <UTC timestamp>-<pid>-<script base>, which matches this filename (tools/ecs/ecsx.sh:103). It ran in the aa-cis-dev-api container as cis_app. At line 13 the script ran `SELECT status, result, last_error FROM shared.job WHERE id=$1`, but shared.job has no last_error column. The column is named `error` (docs/architecture/db-schema-reference.md:12317-12339). The script had imported app code that runs init_sentry() with service=api (api/main.py:136 -> shared/sentry_init.py:250). The uncaught exception therefore reached Sentry through the excepthook and was filed as an aa-cis-api issue. No code on CIS origin/main reads shared.job.last_error: the last_error hits in admin_a4.py:205 and v1_publish.py:1103 belong to other tables (publish log). The product path that ran just before, the INSERT INTO shared.job enqueue, succeeded.

Breadcrumbs: connect as db.user=cis_app -> INSERT INTO shared.job (kind, payload, idempotency_key, ...) succeeded -> the failing SELECT. The shared.job columns in the live schema dump include `error text` and no last_error. `git grep last_error origin/main` in AA-CIS-App finds no query against shared.job.
